cim: San José State Adopts a People-First AI Strategy
cim_eredeti: San José State Adopts a People-First AI Strategy
szoveg_eredeti:
When San José State University’s IT office launched its AdoptAI Champions series, it started by asking staff what obstacles make their jobs difficult.

“We didn’t start with the technology,” says Vincent J. Del Casino Jr., provost and senior vice president of academic affairs at SJSU. “We started with the questions.”

That approach shapes how the university handles artificial intelligence adoption across campus, from staff workflows and faculty development to student use. Rather than layering AI tools onto existing processes, SJSU asks what problem needs solving.

The strategy is a work in progress, Del Casino says, but a few years into the effort, he has clear advice for other institutions: “Don’t invest in the technology unless you figured out the human investment first.”

Here’s how SJSU is putting that principle to work.

According to Del Casino, the first step in encouraging adoption among faculty and staff is providing the professional development they need to use artificial intelligence effectively.

“Often when these kinds of disruptions come in, many faculty and staff are left to just figure it out, so we've built an infrastructure of faculty support,” he says.

On the staff side, where Del Casino says the conversation is “really an agentic AI conversation as much as a generative one,” the AdoptAI Champion series gives employees a place to bring their workflow problems to IT, matching a pain point to a specific solution rather than rolling out generic AI tools.

For faculty, SJSU has a policy requiring every instructor to address AI use in their syllabus, stating how it can — and cannot — be used in their courses. Students need to know where each faculty member stands, Del Casino says.

Alongside that requirement, the institution has committed to training. AI ambassadors now work in every college and most academic programs, running train-the-trainer sessions. And the Center for Faculty Excellence in Teaching Innovation shows instructors how to use the latest AI tools and addresses the challenges that come with each.

EXPLORE: University AI task forces seek input from experts across campus.

Faculty sentiment on AI ranges from those who look for opportunities to weave AI into their classrooms and administrative work to those who want nothing to do with the technology. Del Casino says it’s important to him that SJSU provides space for the conversation and debate without making institutionwide decisions on the matter.

Even if faculty don’t want to use AI, they need to understand how it is changing the classroom, teaching and learning, and adjust their assessments accordingly, he says.

“There are those who are still really skeptical, and rightly so, because there's a lot to be skeptical about,” Del Casino says. “But they’re just asked to talk to the students about it.”

The university is also shaping its faculty from the hiring side. Three years ago, SJSU set a goal that at least 50% of tenure-track hires be at the intersection of AI, machine learning, science and technology studies. Those hires span education, health and the social sciences, and Del Casino says they bring pointed questions about ethical responsibility and guardrails into their departments.

READ MORE: AI is changing campus security.

Del Casino acknowledges that there’s still a lot to learn about AI, and higher education institutions have a responsibility to drive that learning process.

“This is going to be messy for a long time,” he says. “The point of higher education is actually to stay messy and let people struggle. We want to bring a disparate number of voices together and say, ‘All right, where do we stand and sit?’”

The conversations happening among faculty are reaching the students, who have been waiting for clear answers. Like faculty and staff, students’ feelings on AI vary.

“I think the sentiment among some students is everyone should have some basic training in AI literacy. In fact, the university should mandate it,” Del Casino says. “And then there are others who are as skeptical as faculty and say, ‘We're really concerned about what this is going to do to us socially, culturally, politically and economically.’ A lot of them are seeking out support in how to use these tools effectively, and we're trying to respond to that as quickly as possible.”

In response, the university has created a suite of curricular and co-curricular learning experiences for students, including a partnership with IBM to deliver their SkillsBuild program to students. There is also an AI literacy course that the university is looking to embed into Canvas so students can complete it at their own pace.

Faculty are embedding AI education into their curriculum, and individual departments are also tackling the issue.

“Early on, the Writing Center created something called the AI Writers Toolbox, and it was generated by faculty and staff in response to students who were asking, ‘How are we going to be allowed to use these tools?’” Del Casino says.

As an Adobe Creative Campus, SJSU trains students on creative tools, which leads to further ethical conversations about generative AI — a topic that is important to SJSU students.

According to Del Casino, the fastest-growing student group is the Responsible Computing Club. With more than 300 members, the interdisciplinary club aims to study, question and understand the effects of technology.

“The students are going to push us to do this, and we should listen to them so that they have a world that they feel really good about,” Del Casino says.

While most of the AI technology SJSU uses is tied to systemwide contracts through California State University, Del Casino says it’s more important to consider how they’re using the tools they’re given. First and foremost, make sure you have the people to support it.

“One of the most important questions I ask when any tech company comes in is, ‘How many full-time employees do I need to support what you want to sell me?’” he says.

UP NEXT: Universities lean into existing investments when adopting AI tools.

At a Cal State campus with limited resources, he sees AI as a way to free experienced staff from process-heavy work so they can spend more time with students and faculty.

“You don’t solve that with agentic AI,” he says. “You support it with agentic AI, if it’s right and if you’re asking the right questions.”

Ultimately, Del Casino says, the goal is to make sure everyone on campus — students, faculty and staff — knows how to use technology effectively. Starting with the problem also shapes how students approach technology after they graduate.

“When you do that, you’re going to have an incredibly well-trained student group,” he says. “Students are going to go out in the world and hopefully bring that mentality to bear in the broader market.”
